1. Many young professionals suffer from burnout because of constant pressure at work. — BURNOUT (n) = kiệt sức vì công việc; collocation "chronic workplace burnout", "suffer from burnout", "prevent burnout".

2. More and more people are joining the gig economy rather than taking a fixed full-time position. — GIG ECONOMY (n phrase) = nền kinh tế việc làm tự do, ngắn hạn; collocation "join the gig economy", "gig-economy work/platforms". Lưu ý viết đúng hai từ tách rời.

3. Since the pandemic, many companies have normalised telecommuting instead of requiring employees to commute to the office. — TELECOMMUTING (n) = làm việc từ xa; collocation "normalise telecommuting", "telecommuting arrangements", "opt for telecommuting".

4. Employees who are granted autonomy over their schedule tend to feel more motivated. — AUTONOMY (n) = quyền tự chủ; collocation "workplace autonomy", "grant autonomy", "enjoy autonomy over one's schedule".

5. Being a doctor or a lawyer is often seen as a highly lucrative career. — LUCRATIVE (adj) = sinh lời cao, hái ra tiền; collocation "a lucrative career", "lucrative salary", "highly lucrative industry".

6. The job market has become highly volatile, with some industries growing fast while others shrink suddenly. — VOLATILE (adj) = biến động thất thường; collocation "volatile job market", "volatile income", "highly volatile".

7. Workers whose jobs are threatened by automation need reskilling programmes to learn a completely new set of skills. — RESKILLING (n) = đào tạo lại kỹ năng mới; collocation "continuous reskilling", "reskilling pathways", "invest in reskilling".

8. Some employees complain that their manager resorts to micromanagement, checking every small detail of their work. — MICROMANAGEMENT (n) = quản lý vi mô, kiểm soát quá chi tiết; collocation "intrusive micromanagement", "resort to micromanagement", "suffer from micromanagement".

9. The company offers competitive remuneration to attract talented graduates. — REMUNERATION (n) = tiền thù lao, đãi ngộ; collocation "competitive/generous remuneration", "annual remuneration package".

10. In some workplaces, promotion follows a meritocratic system based purely on ability and results. — MERITOCRATIC (adj) = dựa trên năng lực; collocation "a meritocratic system", "meritocratic promotion/culture".

11. Workers in precarious employment often live with the constant worry of losing their income overnight. — PRECARIOUS (adj) = bấp bênh, thiếu ổn định; collocation "precarious employment", "precarious gig-economy work", "a precarious position".

12. After fifteen years in the same role, she decided to take a sabbatical to travel and rest. — SABBATICAL (n) = kỳ nghỉ dài hạn không lương/có lương để nghỉ ngơi hoặc học tập; collocation "take a sabbatical", "a year-long sabbatical", "sabbatical leave".

passages.text: Forecasts of mass technological unemployment have a long, repeatedly disappointed history, and yet the present wave of generative software has revived the debate in a form that earlier sceptics did not anticipate. A more recent generation of labour economists has begun to argue, in the writer's view persuasively, that the question is no longer whether automation will reshape professional work but how unevenly it will do so. The story matters not only because livelihoods are at stake, but because the institutions through which work is organised — firms, professions, training systems — are calibrated for a pace of change that the technology may not respect.

The case for treating the current moment as distinctive rests, in the first place, on the kinds of tasks that have become automatable. According to Professor Lena Westergaard, a labour economist at Stockholm University, the previous waves of office automation primarily displaced routine clerical functions: filing, payroll calculation and the lower rungs of accounting. The latest systems, in contrast, perform tasks that until recently sat squarely within the protected core of professional work, including legal drafting, diagnostic triage and code review. Westergaard's argument is that the resulting exposure is not concentrated in the lowest-paid roles, as twentieth-century automation tended to be, but is distributed across the middle and upper layers of the labour market in patterns that older models cannot easily predict.

The empirical dimension is no less interesting. A 2024 study commissioned by the OECD examined task-level inventories for forty-three occupations across nine member states and reported that, on average, roughly thirty-eight per cent of the tasks performed by professional staff could in principle be automated with currently available tools. The figure is widely cited, although Westergaard cautions that "in principle" is doing considerable work in the sentence. Automatable does not mean automated, since adoption depends on regulation, liability rules and the willingness of organisations to redesign workflows, all of which tend to lag the technology by several years. The headline finding nevertheless suggests that the affected population is substantially larger than in previous transitions.

The first sustained critique of the displacement framing has come from researchers who argue that history offers a more reassuring template. Dr Hector Almeida, an economist at the University of Sao Paulo, has pointed out that earlier shocks — the introduction of spreadsheets in the 1980s, of enterprise software in the 1990s, of cloud platforms in the 2000s — were each predicted to hollow out professional employment and each, in the event, raised aggregate hours and wages within roughly a decade. Almeida concedes that the present technology is unusually general, but he resists the idea that generality alone implies displacement. New tools, he notes, tend to expand the scope of what professionals are asked to do, rather than simply replacing the labour required for the old tasks.

These two views are not in direct conflict, but they pull policy attention in different directions. If the central problem is large-scale, rapid displacement, then the appropriate response involves income support, retraining funds and limits on adoption speed. If, on the other hand, the central problem is uneven gains from a broadly favourable transition, then the appropriate response involves competition policy, access to training and the redistribution of productivity gains. Both interpretations could, in principle, accommodate the same headline figures, although they disagree on which features of the labour market most urgently require attention.

A separate strand of research has focused on within-occupation effects. Professor Wei Chen, a sociologist of professions at the National University of Singapore, has argued that the more interesting consequence of generative tools may be the redistribution of tasks within occupations rather than the elimination of occupations themselves. In repeated interview studies with mid-career lawyers, accountants and software engineers, Chen's team has traced how the more routine elements of professional work tend to migrate towards the tools, leaving practitioners with a residue of unusually demanding and unusually rewarding tasks. The migration of routine tasks through the occupational ladder, she suggests, is a quiet revolution in everyday professional practice, and one which the more dramatic narrative of headcount loss tends to overlook.

As with several other strands of labour research, the most interesting recent work has shifted from short-run forecasts to long-term institutional consequences. The training pipelines developed in the twentieth century — apprenticeships, articled clerkships, junior associate positions — generally relied on routine tasks to give early-career staff a route into expert judgement. If those tasks now migrate to software, the question of how the next generation acquires tacit expertise becomes pressing. Some commentators argue that the institutions will adapt, as they have before. Others, more cautiously, suggest that adaptation may take a generation, and that the intervening cohort may find itself competent in the tools without the deeper grounding that earlier cohorts acquired almost as a by-product of unglamorous work.

The writer's own view settles between the extremes. The current wave is neither the long-feared end of professional employment nor a routine extension of earlier patterns. It is an unusually broad case of skill-biased technological change that contains many of the tensions that still trouble labour-market policy: the relationship between productivity and pay, between training investments and short-term margins, between aggregate gains and the distribution of losses. Reading the current transition with these tensions in mind is more useful than treating it as either a familiar story or an unprecedented rupture.

What current research does support is the modest claim that the exposure of professional work to automation is larger and more evenly distributed across the wage ladder than in any previous wave, and that any policy response treating the transition as either trivial or apocalyptic is unlikely to wear well. Whether readers find the resulting reorganisation troubling or promising depends, in the end, on a familiar question: who counts as a worker whose adjustment costs the wider economy is willing to share?

audio_scripts.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is the second instalment in our future-of-work research series, and we'll be looking specifically at the empirical evidence around compressed working-week trials — what the popular press calls the "four-day week". [pause:5s] The conceptual lens I'll draw on is the productivity-density framework developed by Professor Aleksandr Brzezinski — that's B-R-Z-E-Z-I-N-S-K-I, no accent on the Z, and the second Z is silent in his preferred Anglicisation. So Brzezinski. His 2019 monograph, well, reframed compressed-week analysis away from raw hours-worked towards a density-of-output construct. [pause:3s] Right. A brief tense-orientation note before the data. Brzezinski's framework USED TO be operationalised through hours-saved metrics only, NOW the field deploys triangulated mixed-methods designs incorporating self-report, payroll telemetry, and supervisor evaluations, and from 2028 the Reykjavik consortium WILL be rolling out wearable-biometric modules. Past, present, future. For today's purposes I'm focusing on the CURRENT methodological state — that is, the triangulated mixed-methods phase. [pause:3s] Now, the trial cohort I want to anchor the lecture in was first surveyed in 2021 — sorry, let me correct that, 2020; the published descriptive statistics in 2021 covered baseline data collected in 2020. So whenever I refer to the baseline year for the Reykjavik cohort, please record 2020. [pause:3s] Moving to terminology. The construct Brzezinski foregrounds — a sustained capacity to maintain output quality under reduced scheduled hours — is termed "productivity density". You'll encounter related labels in the older literature: efficiency yield, throughput intensity, hours-saved ratio. All of these gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Brzezinski's term. The currently accepted scholarly term is productivity density — p-r-o-d-u-c-t-i-v-i-t-y density. So when the older literature uses efficiency yield or throughput intensity, that's a related but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain is what organisational economists call the "compression-tolerance spectrum". When ethnographers describe how employees respond to four-day schedules, they sketch a graded continuum running from full task-completion through workload-spillover to compensatory overtime. So, you know, you'll see staff who finish their week genuinely on Thursday — that's full task-completion. Or staff who, kinda, end up logging back in Friday evening anyway — that's compensatory overtime. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical term itself. The umbrella term is the compression-tolerance spectrum. [pause:3s] Now, the headline statistics — and this is where I want you to pay close attention, because the quantifiers cluster densely here. Of the four hundred and twenty employees we sampled across nine firms last quarter, MOST reported maintained or improved output — roughly eighty-two per cent. Only a few — about seven per cent — reported a decline in their measurable output, and some — eleven per cent — reported flat or context-dependent results. So maintained-or-improved dominates numerically, but the seven-per-cent decline tail, though small, is theoretically significant. [pause:3s] A second key construct is "productivity oscillation". This refers to a temporal pattern in which weekly output cycles between high-density and low-density states with no clear monotonic trajectory — sometimes within a single quarter. At the Reykjavik trial site, our analysts recorded one hundred and forty documented oscillation episodes across the cohort during one twelve-week period. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that compression linearly reduces overall output is, frankly, not supported. Most of the firms in our sample did NOT exhibit the predicted monotonic decline in weekly output as scheduled hours decreased. Quite the opposite — many showed a U-shaped curve, with a re-engagement spike around week six. So the older "hours-equal-output" hypothesis, which predicts linear erosion under compression, is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I made at the start. That CURRENT triangulated mixed-methods state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in this afternoon's seminar. I want you to focus on the payroll-telemetry protocols specifically, not the biometric futures or the legacy hours-saved instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: compressed-week outcomes are best understood through productivity density, not raw hours; the technical term for sustained output capacity under reduced hours is productivity density; maintained-or-improved output dominates at roughly eighty-two per cent; and the hours-equal-output hypothesis is not empirically supported in this cohort. Next week we'll examine remote-work geography. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

blocks.text: The line graph illustrates the workforce participation rates of four age cohorts in a developed OECD economy across a forty-year span, with figures recorded at ten-year intervals from 1984 to 2024.

Overall, a striking divergence is evident: the youngest cohort experienced a sustained contraction, whereas the senior and mature groups expanded considerably. The prime working-age cohort, by contrast, remained relatively flat throughout the entire period.

More specifically, participation among 18-to-24-year-olds fell steadily from 72% in 1984 to just 48% in 2024, a decline of 24 percentage points. The 65-and-over cohort, meanwhile, trebled its participation, climbing from a marginal 8% to 24%, with the sharpest acceleration occurring after 2004 as later retirement became increasingly common.

As for the remaining groups, prime-age adults aged 25 to 44 hovered in the low eighties, peaking at 84% in 2004 before easing slightly to 81% by the end. Mature workers aged 45 to 64 rose markedly from 58% to 79%, eventually overtaking their youngest counterparts at around 2004 and finishing the period as the second most active group of all.
The multi-line graph delineates the workforce participation rates of four age cohorts in a developed OECD economy over four decades, with observations taken at decennial intervals.

Overall, the data point to a wholesale recomposition of the workforce: participation among the youngest contracted sharply while that of the oldest expanded dramatically, suggesting a fundamental shift in who sustains the labour market. The prime cohort, by contrast, proved remarkably resistant to change.

In detail, the youth bracket suffered a precipitous decline, sliding from 72% to a mere 48% - a 24-point contraction plausibly attributable to automation displacement and prolonged tertiary enrolment. The senior cohort moved in the opposite direction, trebling from 8% to 24%, a trajectory broadly consistent with the proliferation of gig work and inadequate pension provision.

The mature cohort tells the most telling story. Surging from 58% to 79%, it overtook the youth line around 2004 - a structural inversion symptomatic of demographic ageing and labour polarisation. The prime cohort, fluctuating narrowly between 78% and 84%, anchored the chart even as the generational extremes traded places entirely over the four decades.

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: The accelerating rollout of automation has reignited a long-standing debate about the future of work. While optimists insist that intelligent machines will ultimately generate more jobs than they displace, pessimists warn of mass unemployment on a historic scale. In my view, both outcomes are likely to coexist, though the net effect tends to depend heavily on reskilling policy.

Those who hold a positive view point out that previous technological revolutions, from steam power to the internet, eventually expanded the labour market rather than shrinking it. Routine tasks may be automated, but entirely new occupations - data labellers, AI auditors, prompt engineers - have already emerged. Furthermore, by taking over dangerous or repetitive duties, automation arguably allows workers to concentrate on creative, higher-value roles, which in turn boosts overall productivity and wages.

On the other hand, critics argue that today's wave of automation is qualitatively different because algorithms now encroach on cognitive work, not only manual labour. What worries them most is the pace of change: it is the speed of disruption that prevents middle-aged workers, who often lack digital skills, from retraining in time. In economies where the gig sector is expanding, displaced employees frequently slide into precarious freelance roles with stagnant pay and no fringe benefits, which suggests that headline job-creation figures may conceal severe underemployment.

In my opinion, automation is unlikely to cause permanent mass joblessness, provided that governments invest seriously in lifelong reskilling and a robust social safety net. The technology itself is broadly neutral; what truly determines the outcome are the institutions that surround it. Without proactive policy, the optimistic forecast risks remaining largely theoretical for millions of vulnerable workers across many sectors.

That automation will reshape global employment is no longer in dispute; what divides commentators is whether the net outcome will be job-creating abundance or systemic mass unemployment. Having weighed both positions, I contend that the technology itself is broadly job-neutral, yet without aggressive reskilling it almost certainly intensifies labour-market precarity for the bottom quintile of earners.

Proponents of the optimistic view marshal compelling historical evidence. Each prior wave of mechanisation eventually birthed occupations unimaginable to displaced workers, and current OECD modelling suggests a similar pattern: tens of millions of routine roles will vanish, but a comparable number of augmentation roles - AI trainers, ethics officers, human-in-the-loop reviewers - appear poised to absorb the slack. Moreover, by offloading drudgery, intelligent systems plausibly elevate human productivity, freeing employees for the relational and creative work that algorithms still struggle to replicate.

Sceptics, however, raise a structural objection that deserves serious weight. Never before has automation simultaneously targeted cognitive, manual and clerical occupations alike. What this implies is a transition burden falling disproportionately on mid-career workers whose tacit expertise depreciates faster than they can plausibly reskill. Particularly worrying is the fiduciary asymmetry between platform companies and their contractors: gig workers who replace salaried employees inherit volatile incomes, no tenure and minimal social protection, even as the headline statistics flatter the underlying picture.

On balance, I align cautiously with the optimists, but only conditionally. What ultimately determines whether automation enriches or impoverishes is the institutional scaffolding surrounding it - universal reskilling vouchers, robust unemployment insurance and binding standards on algorithmic management. Absent such guardrails, the dividends of automation will accrue overwhelmingly to capital, leaving labour to absorb the volatility and the chronic insecurity that inevitably accompany an unmanaged transition of this magnitude.

Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. Many young professionals suffer from burnout because of constant pressure at work. — BURNOUT (n) = kiệt sức vì công việc; collocation "chronic workplace burnout", "suffer from burnout", "prevent burnout".

2. More and more people are joining the gig economy rather than taking a fixed full-time position. — GIG ECONOMY (n phrase) = nền kinh tế việc làm tự do, ngắn hạn; collocation "join the gig economy", "gig-economy work/platforms". Lưu ý viết đúng hai từ tách rời.

3. Since the pandemic, many companies have normalised telecommuting instead of requiring employees to commute to the office. — TELECOMMUTING (n) = làm việc từ xa; collocation "normalise telecommuting", "telecommuting arrangements", "opt for telecommuting".

4. Employees who are granted autonomy over their schedule tend to feel more motivated. — AUTONOMY (n) = quyền tự chủ; collocation "workplace autonomy", "grant autonomy", "enjoy autonomy over one's schedule".

5. Being a doctor or a lawyer is often seen as a highly lucrative career. — LUCRATIVE (adj) = sinh lời cao, hái ra tiền; collocation "a lucrative career", "lucrative salary", "highly lucrative industry".

6. The job market has become highly volatile, with some industries growing fast while others shrink suddenly. — VOLATILE (adj) = biến động thất thường; collocation "volatile job market", "volatile income", "highly volatile".

7. Workers whose jobs are threatened by automation need reskilling programmes to learn a completely new set of skills. — RESKILLING (n) = đào tạo lại kỹ năng mới; collocation "continuous reskilling", "reskilling pathways", "invest in reskilling".

8. Some employees complain that their manager resorts to micromanagement, checking every small detail of their work. — MICROMANAGEMENT (n) = quản lý vi mô, kiểm soát quá chi tiết; collocation "intrusive micromanagement", "resort to micromanagement", "suffer from micromanagement".

9. The company offers competitive remuneration to attract talented graduates. — REMUNERATION (n) = tiền thù lao, đãi ngộ; collocation "competitive/generous remuneration", "annual remuneration package".

10. In some workplaces, promotion follows a meritocratic system based purely on ability and results. — MERITOCRATIC (adj) = dựa trên năng lực; collocation "a meritocratic system", "meritocratic promotion/culture".

11. Workers in precarious employment often live with the constant worry of losing their income overnight. — PRECARIOUS (adj) = bấp bênh, thiếu ổn định; collocation "precarious employment", "precarious gig-economy work", "a precarious position".

12. After fifteen years in the same role, she decided to take a sabbatical to travel and rest. — SABBATICAL (n) = kỳ nghỉ dài hạn không lương/có lương để nghỉ ngơi hoặc học tập; collocation "take a sabbatical", "a year-long sabbatical", "sabbatical leave".
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu

1. Band 7: A growing number of people are working from home compared with before the pandemic. Band 8: The proportion of the workforce operating remotely has risen markedly since the pandemic, a shift that shows little sign of reversing.

2. Band 7: Automation is expected to replace a considerable number of jobs in the coming years. Band 8: With automation poised to displace a substantial share of routine jobs in the years ahead, the urgency of large-scale reskilling has never been more apparent.

3. Band 7: Companies should provide training programmes so that workers are not made redundant by new technology. Band 8: Unless companies invest proactively in reskilling programmes, a considerable proportion of their workforce risks being rendered redundant by advancing automation.

4. Band 7: Some people opt for a lower-paid job because it brings them greater job satisfaction. Band 8: Rather than chasing the highest salary, some individuals deliberately opt for lower-paid roles that afford them greater autonomy and personal fulfilment.

5. Band 7: Young workers today tend to move between different jobs rather than remaining with one employer for life. Band 8: Unlike previous generations, today's young workers are far more inclined to move fluidly between employers than to commit to a single company for the duration of their career.

6. Band 7: Working excessively long hours without adequate rest can seriously undermine a person's health. Band 8: Chronic overwork, if left unchecked, can precipitate serious physical and psychological health problems, burnout being merely the most visible symptom.

7. Band 7: Women remain considerably less likely than men to reach senior positions in many companies. Band 8: Despite decades of progress, women continue to be disproportionately underrepresented in senior leadership, a persistent barrier often described as the glass ceiling.

8. Band 7: A good manager should trust employees with the autonomy to manage their own time. Band 8: Effective leadership increasingly hinges on granting employees sufficient autonomy to manage their own time, rather than resorting to intrusive micromanagement.

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)

The Automation Threat: The World Economic Forum estimates that AI and automation could displace 85 million jobs globally by 2025, while creating 97 million new ones, underscoring the absolute necessity of reskilling.

The "Great Resignation": A post-pandemic trend where millions of employees quit their jobs voluntarily, citing burnout, toxic workplace cultures (micromanagement), and a demand for remote work flexibility.
The Rise of the Gig Economy: By 2027, over 50% of the US workforce is projected to participate in the gig economy (Uber, Upwork), valuing flexibility over traditional job tenure and pensions.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Job Satisfaction vs. High Salary

For Salary: A lucrative income guarantees financial stability, providing a high standard of living and the ability to afford excellent healthcare/education for one's family; money is a tangible incentive that rewards hard work.

For Satisfaction: A high-paying but highly stressful job inevitably leads to severe burnout and physical ailments; job satisfaction ensures long-term mental well-being, intrinsic motivation, and a healthier work-life balance.
Topic: The Gig Economy (Pros vs. Cons)

Pros (Flexibility): Workers enjoy complete autonomy over their schedules, deciding when and where to work; it provides easy entry into the workforce for students and marginalised groups without navigating strict corporate hiring processes.
Cons (Insecurity): Utter lack of job security (no tenure); zero fringe benefits such as paid sick leave, health insurance, or retirement pensions; income is highly volatile and unpredictable.
Topic: Telecommuting (Remote Work) vs. Office Work
Telecommuting Pros: Eliminates exhausting daily commutes, saving time and reducing a company's overhead costs (rent, electricity); expands the talent pool globally.

Office Work Pros: Fosters spontaneous collaboration and team bonding; establishes a clear physical boundary between professional duties and home life, preventing employees from feeling "snowed under" 24/7.

Model Answer (Band 7.5-8.0, ~270 words)

What I'd like to discuss is the role of the bank teller — a profession that, in my considered view, is teetering on the brink of obsolescence and may well vanish within the coming decade. Bank tellers, for those unfamiliar, are the front-desk staff who process cash deposits, withdrawals, and routine account enquiries — essentially the human face of retail banking.

The reasoning behind my prediction boils down to a confluence of technological and behavioural shifts. Firstly, what automation has fundamentally done is hollow out the routine, rule-based tasks that constituted the bulk of a teller's daily workload. Mobile banking apps and AI-powered chatbots now handle the lion's share of transactions, with some industry estimates suggesting that a large share of teller activities are already automatable. Secondly, in Vietnam, cashless transactions have surged sharply in recent years, which has rendered the physical branch increasingly redundant.

Compounding this is the issue of precarity in the sector — banks like HSBC and Citibank have been quietly shuttering branches and reskilling staff, while neobanks such as Timo and Cake operate with virtually no physical footprint whatsoever. What this represents, arguably, is not merely a job category disappearing but an entire mode of customer-facing labour being decoupled from human presence.

The societal ramifications, I'd suggest, are double-edged. On the one hand, displaced workers — often middle-aged women without robust digital skills — face genuine hardship and the spectre of long-term unemployment. On the other hand, the freed-up human capital could, in theory, be redeployed into higher-value advisory roles, provided governments fund meaningful retraining.
All things considered, the bank teller's fate epitomises the broader anxieties of the automation era.

sections.title: PART 2 — Cue Card: Describe a job that you think will disappear in the future

blocks.text: Q1: Will universal basic income become necessary?

Point: I'd cautiously argue that some form of universal basic income, or UBI, will become not just desirable but structurally necessary within the next two or three decades — though the specifics of implementation remain genuinely contested.

Explain: The crux of the matter is that if automation displaces 85 million jobs globally by 2025, as the World Economic Forum projects, then the traditional link between paid employment and basic subsistence may simply collapse for a sizeable minority. UBI offers a buffer against this precarity, decoupling survival from the increasingly volatile labour market.

Example: Finland's two-year UBI pilot from 2017, which paid 2,000 unemployed citizens €560 monthly, found that recipients experienced significantly lower stress and modestly improved employment outcomes — though the scheme wasn't scaled up due to political pushback. Conversely, Stockton, California's SEED programme demonstrated that recipients spent the money on essentials like food and utilities, debunking the lazy stereotype of welfare dependency.

Link: So while UBI is no panacea, it's increasingly being viewed as a pragmatic response to structural unemployment rather than a utopian fantasy — and policymakers who ignore it do so at their peril.
Q2: Should governments retrain displaced workers?

Point: Yes, unequivocally — government-funded reskilling isn't merely a moral obligation; it's an economic imperative if we're to avoid the social fractures that have historically accompanied technological revolutions.

Explain: What's at stake is essentially the social contract: when automation generates wealth concentrated in the hands of capital owners while leaving workers stranded, the resulting inequality fuels populism and erodes democratic stability. Targeted reskilling redistributes opportunity rather than just income.

Example: Singapore's SkillsFuture initiative, launched in 2015, gives every citizen aged 25-plus a S$500 credit for accredited courses, with top-ups for mid-career workers — and a substantial number of Singaporeans access training each year. Denmark's flexicurity model goes even further, combining easy hiring-and-firing with generous retraining stipends, which has kept unemployment below 5% despite rapid sectoral churn.
Link: Ultimately, leaving displaced workers to fend for themselves is both ethically bankrupt and economically self-defeating; structured reskilling is the only credible path forward.
Q3: Is remote work the new normal?

Point: Remote work has, in my view, established itself as a permanent fixture of the professional landscape, though the more accurate description would be hybrid rather than fully remote — at least for knowledge workers.

Explain: The fundamental shift is that the pandemic effectively conducted a global experiment that, almost overnight, normalised telecommuting and demonstrated that productivity needn't be tethered to a physical office. What employers have realised is that imposing rigid five-day returns triggers attrition, particularly among high-performing staff.

Example: Research on hybrid-work arrangements — typically two to three days remote — suggests they can boost productivity while reducing staff attrition. In Vietnam, FPT Software and VNG have institutionalised flexible policies, citing both talent retention and overhead savings. That said, junior employees often benefit from in-person mentorship, which fully remote setups struggle to replicate.
Link: So while remote work isn't universally applicable, the genie is firmly out of the bottle — and organisations clinging to pre-2020 norms will increasingly find themselves outmanoeuvred.

> Good morning. Today's lecture dismantles three comforting myths circulating in contemporary labour economics: that the gig economy liberates workers, that labour-market polarisation is transient, and that automation displacement can be left to market forces. Each, I will contend, is empirically untenable.

> Consider, first, the gig-economy narrative. Platforms such as Uber, Deliveroo and Upwork sell algorithmically mediated flexibility — the dignity, supposedly, of being one's own boss. The shadow ledger reads rather differently. Drivers and couriers absorb the fixed costs of vehicles, fuel and insurance while shouldering income volatility and forfeiting statutory entitlements — paid leave, pensions, collective bargaining. A 2021 study by the JPMorgan Chase Institute found that gig income for the median platform worker fluctuated by forty-seven percent month-on-month. Flexibility, in short, is repackaged precarity.

> Now, labour-market polarisation. The MIT economist David Autor demonstrated that demand has grown at the high-skill apex — analysts, surgeons, software architects — and at the low-skill base, in care work and food service. The middle — clerical roles, routine assembly, mid-tier administration — has been hollowed out by software automation. The graduate, paradoxically, sometimes ends up tending bar.

> Finally, automation displacement. The World Economic Forum projects that eighty-five million roles will be displaced globally by 2025, while ninety-seven million new roles emerge. Net positive, yes — but the displaced rarely transition seamlessly into the new occupations. Without aggressive public investment in reskilling pathways and portable benefits, the transition will be distributionally brutal.

Now, before figure four, I want to anticipate the optimist in the room — the one who says, well, every previous wave of automation eventually generated more employment than it destroyed, so why panic this time? It is a fair challenge, and it deserves a serious answer rather than a dismissal. The historical analogy people reach for is the agricultural transition: two centuries ago, the overwhelming majority of workers tilled fields; today a tiny fraction does, yet we are not mired in mass unemployment. The labour simply migrated.

But — and here is the crux — that migration took generations, and it was anything but painless for those living through it. [pause] The Luddites were not irrational technophobes; they were skilled artisans watching their wage premium evaporate within a single working lifetime. The economic historian Robert Allen calls this the "Engels pause" — a stretch of decades in early industrialisation during which output soared while real wages for ordinary workers flatlined. The aggregate statistics looked magnificent; the lived experience was grim.

What troubles contemporary economists is the question of speed and scope. Earlier automation displaced muscle; large language models now encroach on cognitive, even creative, tasks — drafting, summarising, coding, diagnosing. Erik Brynjolfsson has flagged the worry that, um, the technology may be skill-biased in unpredictable directions, sometimes assisting the novice, sometimes the expert, rarely both evenly. [pause] So we cannot simply assume the new roles will land in the same regions, or with the same people, as the displaced ones.

And there is a subtler point about measurement. We obsess over jobs lost and jobs created, but the more consequential variable may be wage-setting power — whether workers retain leverage to capture a share of the productivity gains at all. A net-positive headcount is cold comfort if the new roles pay less and bargain weaker. Which brings us squarely to the institutional question the next section must confront, namely…
> The conclusion is sobering: technology never simply liberates labour; it redistributes risk. Now, turning to figure four, which traces wage divergence since 1980…

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~175 từ)
The line graph illustrates the workforce participation rates of four age cohorts in a developed OECD economy across a forty-year span, with figures recorded at ten-year intervals from 1984 to 2024.

Overall, a striking divergence is evident: the youngest cohort experienced a sustained contraction, whereas the senior and mature groups expanded considerably. The prime working-age cohort, by contrast, remained relatively flat throughout the entire period.

More specifically, participation among 18-to-24-year-olds fell steadily from 72% in 1984 to just 48% in 2024, a decline of 24 percentage points. The 65-and-over cohort, meanwhile, trebled its participation, climbing from a marginal 8% to 24%, with the sharpest acceleration occurring after 2004 as later retirement became increasingly common.

As for the remaining groups, prime-age adults aged 25 to 44 hovered in the low eighties, peaking at 84% in 2004 before easing slightly to 81% by the end. Mature workers aged 45 to 64 rose markedly from 58% to 79%, eventually overtaking their youngest counterparts at around 2004 and finishing the period as the second most active group of all.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~181 từ)
The multi-line graph delineates the workforce participation rates of four age cohorts in a developed OECD economy over four decades, with observations taken at decennial intervals.

Overall, the data point to a wholesale recomposition of the workforce: participation among the youngest contracted sharply while that of the oldest expanded dramatically, suggesting a fundamental shift in who sustains the labour market. The prime cohort, by contrast, proved remarkably resistant to change.

In detail, the youth bracket suffered a precipitous decline, sliding from 72% to a mere 48% - a 24-point contraction plausibly attributable to automation displacement and prolonged tertiary enrolment. The senior cohort moved in the opposite direction, trebling from 8% to 24%, a trajectory broadly consistent with the proliferation of gig work and inadequate pension provision.

The mature cohort tells the most telling story. Surging from 58% to 79%, it overtook the youth line around 2004 - a structural inversion symptomatic of demographic ageing and labour polarisation. The prime cohort, fluctuating narrowly between 78% and 84%, anchored the chart even as the generational extremes traded places entirely over the four decades.

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~277 words)

The accelerating rollout of automation has reignited a long-standing debate about the future of work. While optimists insist that intelligent machines will ultimately generate more jobs than they displace, pessimists warn of mass unemployment on a historic scale. In my view, both outcomes are likely to coexist, though the net effect tends to depend heavily on reskilling policy.

Those who hold a positive view point out that previous technological revolutions, from steam power to the internet, eventually expanded the labour market rather than shrinking it. Routine tasks may be automated, but entirely new occupations - data labellers, AI auditors, prompt engineers - have already emerged. Furthermore, by taking over dangerous or repetitive duties, automation arguably allows workers to concentrate on creative, higher-value roles, which in turn boosts overall productivity and wages.

On the other hand, critics argue that today's wave of automation is qualitatively different because algorithms now encroach on cognitive work, not only manual labour. What worries them most is the pace of change: it is the speed of disruption that prevents middle-aged workers, who often lack digital skills, from retraining in time. In economies where the gig sector is expanding, displaced employees frequently slide into precarious freelance roles with stagnant pay and no fringe benefits, which suggests that headline job-creation figures may conceal severe underemployment.

In my opinion, automation is unlikely to cause permanent mass joblessness, provided that governments invest seriously in lifelong reskilling and a robust social safety net. The technology itself is broadly neutral; what truly determines the outcome are the institutions that surround it. Without proactive policy, the optimistic forecast risks remaining largely theoretical for millions of vulnerable workers across many sectors.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~287 words)

That automation will reshape global employment is no longer in dispute; what divides commentators is whether the net outcome will be job-creating abundance or systemic mass unemployment. Having weighed both positions, I contend that the technology itself is broadly job-neutral, yet without aggressive reskilling it almost certainly intensifies labour-market precarity for the bottom quintile of earners.

Proponents of the optimistic view marshal compelling historical evidence. Each prior wave of mechanisation eventually birthed occupations unimaginable to displaced workers, and current OECD modelling suggests a similar pattern: tens of millions of routine roles will vanish, but a comparable number of augmentation roles - AI trainers, ethics officers, human-in-the-loop reviewers - appear poised to absorb the slack. Moreover, by offloading drudgery, intelligent systems plausibly elevate human productivity, freeing employees for the relational and creative work that algorithms still struggle to replicate.

Sceptics, however, raise a structural objection that deserves serious weight. Never before has automation simultaneously targeted cognitive, manual and clerical occupations alike. What this implies is a transition burden falling disproportionately on mid-career workers whose tacit expertise depreciates faster than they can plausibly reskill. Particularly worrying is the fiduciary asymmetry between platform companies and their contractors: gig workers who replace salaried employees inherit volatile incomes, no tenure and minimal social protection, even as the headline statistics flatter the underlying picture.

On balance, I align cautiously with the optimists, but only conditionally. What ultimately determines whether automation enriches or impoverishes is the institutional scaffolding surrounding it - universal reskilling vouchers, robust unemployment insurance and binding standards on algorithmic management. Absent such guardrails, the dividends of automation will accrue overwhelmingly to capital, leaving labour to absorb the volatility and the chronic insecurity that inevitably accompany an unmanaged transition of this magnitude.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dẫn bằng chứng cụ thể hơn (OECD modelling, augmentation roles cụ thể) và nominalisation dày đặc ('transition burden', 'institutional scaffolding', 'fiduciary asymmetry'), nâng Task Response và Lexical Resource.
•  Band 8 có cohesion liền mạch với connector tinh tế ('Particularly worrying is', 'Absent such guardrails') và register học thuật nhất quán, loại bỏ cụm đời thường như 'taking over' của bản 7.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quyền được tự chủ, tự quyết định cách thức làm việc mà không bị giám sát chặt chẽ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Greater workplace **autonomy** has been shown to enhance both productivity and job satisfaction.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Auto-' (tự) cộng '-nomy' (luật, quy tắc) nghĩa là tự đặt ra luật cho bản thân, tức tự chủ.
vocabulary.common_error: Phân biệt với 'autocracy' (chế độ chuyên quyền) — hai từ gần giống mặt chữ nhưng nghĩa trái ngược hoàn toàn.
vocabulary.definition_en: the freedom to act and make decisions independently, without close supervision
vocabulary.definition_vi: quyền tự chủ, sự tự do quyết định trong công việc
vocabulary.example: Working independently without a boss constantly checking on you — that is, enjoying genuine workplace autonomy — makes employees more productive.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Auto-' (tự) + '-nomy' (luật, quy tắc) = tự đặt ra luật cho bản thân, tức tự chủ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tính từ mô tả một công việc hoặc hoạt động mang lại lợi nhuận, thu nhập cao.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> He quit his **lucrative** job because, although it paid a great deal of money, it led to severe burnout.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc 'lucr-' trong tiếng Latin liên quan đến tiền lời, nên 'lucrative' luôn gợi hình ảnh kiếm được nhiều tiền.
vocabulary.common_error: *Lucrative* nghĩa là sinh lợi, không chỉ lương cao; tránh cụm thừa *lucrative and profitable*.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of a business, job, or activity) producing a great deal of profit; very profitable
vocabulary.definition_vi: sinh lời cao, mang lại nhiều lợi nhuận
vocabulary.example: He quit his lucrative job because, although it paid a great deal of money, it led to severe burnout.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Lucr-' gốc Latin liên quan đến 'tiền lời' — 'lucrative' luôn đi kèm hình ảnh kiếm được nhiều tiền.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tính từ mô tả sự biến động, thay đổi nhanh và khó lường, thường theo chiều hướng xấu.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The job market changes very fast and has become entirely **volatile** in the age of automation.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Liên tưởng 'volatile' với chất hoá học dễ bay hơi, biến đổi bất ngờ, giống như thị trường việc làm bấp bênh.
vocabulary.common_error: Không nhầm 'volatile' (biến động) với 'voluntary' (tự nguyện) — hai từ dễ gây nhầm lẫn về mặt âm.
vocabulary.definition_en: liable to change rapidly and unpredictably, especially for the worse
vocabulary.definition_vi: bấp bênh, biến động thất thường (khó lường trước)
vocabulary.example: The job market changes very fast and has become entirely volatile in the age of automation.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Liên tưởng 'volatile' với chất hoá học dễ bay hơi, biến đổi bất ngờ — thị trường việc làm cũng vậy.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Việc đào tạo lại để người lao động có kỹ năng mới, phù hợp với công việc hoặc công nghệ mới.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Because of AI, workers need continuous **reskilling** to remain relevant in the labour market.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Re-' (lại) cộng 'skill' (kỹ năng) nghĩa là học lại kỹ năng từ đầu cho một công việc khác.
vocabulary.common_error: Phân biệt 'reskilling' (học kỹ năng MỚI để đổi nghề) với 'upskilling' (nâng cao kỹ năng HIỆN CÓ trong cùng nghề).
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of teaching employees new skills so they can do a different job or adapt to new technologies
vocabulary.definition_vi: quá trình đào tạo lại kỹ năng mới cho người lao động
vocabulary.example: Because of AI, workers need continuous reskilling to remain relevant in the labour market.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Re-' (lại) + 'skill' (kỹ năng) = học lại kỹ năng từ đầu cho một công việc khác.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cách quản lý kiểm soát quá chi tiết, khiến nhân viên mất đi sự tự chủ trong công việc.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The project failed due to the manager's constant and intrusive **micromanagement**, which destroyed team morale.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Micro-' (nhỏ, chi tiết) cộng 'management' nghĩa là quản lý đến từng chi tiết nhỏ nhặt, khiến nhân viên ngột ngạt.
vocabulary.common_error: *Micromanagement* là danh từ không đếm được; người thực hiện là *a micromanager*, động từ là *micromanage*.
vocabulary.definition_en: management with excessive control over or attention to detail, which undermines employees' independence
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự quản lý vi mô, kiểm soát quá mức làm mất đi tính tự chủ của nhân viên
vocabulary.example: The project failed due to the manager's constant and intrusive micromanagement, which destroyed team morale.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Micro-' (nhỏ, chi tiết) + 'management' = quản lý đến từng chi tiết nhỏ nhặt, khiến nhân viên ngột ngạt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khoản tiền công, thù lao trả cho công sức lao động, thường dùng trong văn phong trang trọng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Competitive **remuneration** is a key lever for attracting and retaining skilled employees.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Re-' (lại) cộng gốc Latin 'munus' (quà, nghĩa vụ) nghĩa là trả lại công sức bằng tiền, tức thù lao.
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là danh từ trang trọng, không dùng động từ 'remunerate' trong văn nói thông thường; văn nói dùng 'pay' hoặc 'salary'.
vocabulary.definition_en: money paid for work or services rendered; salary or compensation
vocabulary.definition_vi: thù lao, tiền công/lương
vocabulary.example: Competitive remuneration is a key lever for attracting and retaining skilled employees.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Re-' (lại) + gốc Latin 'munus' (quà, nghĩa vụ) = trả lại công sức bằng tiền, tức thù lao.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tính từ mô tả một hệ thống trọng dụng người có năng lực thay vì dựa vào quan hệ hay đặc quyền.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A truly **meritocratic** system rewards talent and effort rather than family connections.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Merit' (công trạng, năng lực) cộng '-cratic' (cai trị) nghĩa là một hệ thống nơi năng lực quyết định vị trí.
vocabulary.common_error: Không nhầm với 'democratic' — 'meritocratic' liên quan đến năng lực (merit), không liên quan đến bầu cử hay dân chủ.
vocabulary.definition_en: based on the principle that advancement should depend on ability and achievement rather than privilege or connections
vocabulary.definition_vi: trọng dụng tài năng, dựa trên năng lực thực sự
vocabulary.example: A truly meritocratic system rewards talent and effort rather than family connections.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Merit' (công trạng, năng lực) + '-cratic' (cai trị) = một hệ thống nơi năng lực quyết định vị trí.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tính từ mô tả tình trạng việc làm hoặc vị trí bấp bênh, không có sự đảm bảo lâu dài.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> An expanding share of the workforce is trapped in **precarious**, gig-economy employment with no job security.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Liên tưởng đến việc đứng trên vách đá chông chênh, dễ rơi — giống một công việc không ổn định.
vocabulary.common_error: *Precarious* nhấn mạnh thiếu ổn định/an toàn; không nhầm với *precious* và thường đi với *employment, position, situation*.
vocabulary.definition_en: not securely held or in position; likely to fall or be lost, especially referring to insecure employment
vocabulary.definition_vi: bấp bênh, thiếu an toàn, thiếu ổn định (về việc làm)
vocabulary.example: An expanding share of the workforce is trapped in precarious, gig-economy employment with no job security.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Liên tưởng đến việc đứng trên vách đá 'precarious' — chông chênh, dễ rơi, giống việc làm không ổn định.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Việc nâng cao, cải thiện kỹ năng chuyên môn hiện có để đáp ứng yêu cầu công việc cao hơn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Continuous **upskilling** is indispensable in an increasingly automated labour market.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Up-' (lên) cộng 'skill' nghĩa là nâng kỹ năng lên một tầm cao mới trong công việc hiện tại.
vocabulary.common_error: Phân biệt 'upskilling' (nâng cao kỹ năng CÙNG nghề) với 'reskilling' (học kỹ năng MỚI để đổi nghề).
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of teaching employees additional skills to improve their performance in their current role
vocabulary.definition_vi: nâng cao kỹ năng hiện có để làm việc tốt hơn trong cùng lĩnh vực
vocabulary.example: Continuous upskilling is indispensable in an increasingly automated labour market.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Up-' (lên) + 'skill' = nâng kỹ năng lên một tầm cao mới trong công việc hiện tại.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Kỳ nghỉ dài hạn được cấp cho nhân viên, thường nhằm mục đích học tập, du lịch hoặc nghỉ ngơi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> After a decade of relentless work, she decided to take a **sabbatical** to recover from burnout and pursue further study.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc từ 'Sabbath' (ngày nghỉ) cho thấy 'sabbatical' là một kỳ nghỉ dài để phục hồi, giống ngày nghỉ được kéo dài ra.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *take/go on a sabbatical*; không gọi mọi kỳ nghỉ ngắn là *sabbatical* vì từ này thường chỉ thời gian nghỉ dài có mục đích.
vocabulary.definition_en: an extended period of leave granted to an employee, often for study, travel, or rest
vocabulary.definition_vi: kỳ nghỉ dài hạn (thường để học tập hoặc nghỉ ngơi)
vocabulary.example: After a decade of relentless work, she decided to take a sabbatical to recover from burnout and pursue further study.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc từ 'Sabbath' (ngày nghỉ trong tuần) — 'sabbatical' là kỳ nghỉ dài để phục hồi, giống ngày nghỉ được kéo dài ra.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tính từ mô tả tinh thần dám khởi nghiệp, sáng tạo và chấp nhận rủi ro để theo đuổi cơ hội kinh doanh.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The company is looking for young people with a strong **entrepreneurial** spirit who can identify opportunities and take risks.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Từ gốc Pháp 'entreprendre' (thực hiện, dấn thân) cho thấy người có tinh thần này luôn dấn thân vào ý tưởng mới.
vocabulary.common_error: Chú ý chính tả: 'entrepreneurial' có 'e' sau 'entrepr-', dễ viết thiếu hoặc thừa nguyên âm.
vocabulary.definition_en: having the characteristics of someone who sets up businesses, taking on financial risk in pursuit of profit; showing initiative and innovation
vocabulary.definition_vi: có tinh thần khởi nghiệp, dám nghĩ dám làm
vocabulary.example: The company is looking for young people with a strong entrepreneurial spirit who can identify opportunities and take risks.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Từ gốc Pháp 'entreprendre' (thực hiện, dấn thân) — người có tinh thần 'entrepreneurial' luôn dấn thân vào ý tưởng mới.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Redundancy nghĩa là tình trạng bị mất việc vì công ty không còn cần vị trí đó nữa, thường do tái cơ cấu.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Thousands of factory workers faced **redundancy** after the plant automated most of its production line.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Redundant' nghĩa là dư thừa, không cần thiết, nên 'redundancy' là tình trạng trở nên dư thừa và bị cho thôi việc.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Redundancy' (Anh-Anh, mất việc do dôi dư vị trí) khác với 'unemployment' (thất nghiệp nói chung, không chỉ rõ nguyên nhân).
vocabulary.definition_en: The situation of losing one's job because an employer no longer needs it, typically due to restructuring or cost-cutting.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Tình trạng bị dôi dư, mất việc do tái cơ cấu hoặc cắt giảm nhân sự
vocabulary.example: Thousands of factory workers faced redundancy after the plant automated most of its production line.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Redundant' nghĩa là dư thừa, không cần thiết → 'redundancy' là tình trạng trở nên dư thừa trong công ty và bị cho thôi việc.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vocational nghĩa là thuộc về hướng nghiệp hoặc đào tạo kỹ năng thực hành cho một công việc cụ thể.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Rather than pursuing a traditional degree, many young people now opt for **vocational** training in high-demand trades.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Vocation' nghĩa là nghề nghiệp/thiên chức, nên 'vocational' là những gì liên quan đến việc đào tạo cho một nghề cụ thể.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'vocational' (liên quan đến đào tạo nghề, kỹ năng thực hành) với 'vocal' (thuộc về giọng nói).
vocabulary.definition_en: Relating to an occupation or specific practical skills needed for a particular job, rather than academic study.
vocabulary.definition_vi: Thuộc về hướng nghiệp, đào tạo nghề (kỹ năng thực hành cho công việc cụ thể)
vocabulary.example: Rather than pursuing a traditional degree, many young people now opt for vocational training in high-demand trades.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Vocation' (thiên chức, nghề nghiệp) + '-al' → 'vocational' là những gì liên quan trực tiếp đến việc đào tạo cho một nghề cụ thể.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thành ngữ diễn tả việc thăng tiến dần dần qua các vị trí cao hơn trong sự nghiệp.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> He worked incredibly hard to **climb the corporate ladder** and eventually become the CEO.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình dung một chiếc thang trong công ty — mỗi bậc thang là một cấp bậc, càng leo cao càng thăng tiến.
collocations: work one's way up the ladder
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm cố định là *climb the corporate ladder*; không dùng *climb on the ladder* trong nghĩa thăng tiến sự nghiệp.
vocabulary.definition_en: to progress steadily through a series of increasingly senior positions within a company or organisation
vocabulary.definition_vi: leo lên nấc thang sự nghiệp, thăng tiến trong công ty
vocabulary.example: He worked incredibly hard to climb the corporate ladder and eventually become the CEO.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung một chiếc thang (ladder) trong công ty — mỗi bậc thang là một cấp bậc, càng leo cao càng thăng tiến.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thành ngữ diễn tả tình trạng bị quá tải, ngập trong khối lượng công việc lớn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> I can't come to the party tonight; I am completely **snowed under** with paperwork.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình dung bị chôn vùi dưới một lớp tuyết dày, giống như bị công việc chất chồng lên người.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *be snowed under with work/paperwork*; không dùng *snowed under by work* trong mẫu thông dụng.
vocabulary.definition_en: overwhelmed with a large amount of work to deal with
vocabulary.definition_vi: ngập đầu trong công việc, quá tải công việc
vocabulary.example: I can't come to the party tonight; I am completely snowed under with paperwork.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung bị chôn vùi dưới một lớp tuyết dày (snowed under) — giống như bị công việc chất chồng lên người.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cụm từ chỉ một công việc không có triển vọng phát triển hay thăng tiến trong tương lai.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> She felt trapped in a **dead-end job** with absolutely no prospects for promotion.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Dead end' nghĩa đen là ngõ cụt — một công việc dead-end cũng giống như đi vào ngõ cụt, không lối thoát để thăng tiến.
vocabulary.common_error: Cần dấu gạch nối trong *dead-end job*; cụm chỉ công việc không có triển vọng thăng tiến, không đơn thuần là công việc khó.
vocabulary.definition_en: a job with no prospects of advancement or improvement
vocabulary.definition_vi: công việc bế tắc, không có cơ hội thăng tiến
vocabulary.example: She felt trapped in a dead-end job with absolutely no prospects for promotion.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Dead end' nghĩa đen là ngõ cụt — một công việc 'dead-end' cũng giống như đi vào ngõ cụt, không lối thoát để thăng tiến.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thành ngữ thông tục chỉ việc bị đuổi việc, bị sa thải khỏi công ty.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> If you keep arriving late and missing deadlines, you will eventually **get the sack**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ngày xưa công nhân bị đuổi việc phải nhận lại đồ nghề trong một cái bao tải (sack) — từ đó có thành ngữ này.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Get the sack' là thành ngữ Anh-Anh không trang trọng; trong văn viết học thuật nên dùng 'be dismissed' hoặc 'be made redundant'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to be dismissed from one's job
vocabulary.definition_vi: bị sa thải, bị đuổi việc
vocabulary.example: If you keep arriving late and missing deadlines, you will eventually get the sack.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Ngày xưa công nhân bị đuổi việc phải nhận lại đồ nghề trong một cái bao tải (sack) — từ đó có thành ngữ 'get the sack'.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thành ngữ diễn tả cách suy nghĩ sáng tạo, vượt ra khỏi khuôn khổ thông thường.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Modern employers value candidates who can **think outside the box** to solve complex problems.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình dung một chiếc hộp tượng trưng cho lối suy nghĩ thông thường — thinking outside the box là bước ra khỏi khuôn khổ đó.
collocations: encourage staff to think outside the box
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm cố định là *think outside the box*; không nói *think out of the box* trong chuẩn dùng của bộ học liệu này.
vocabulary.definition_en: to think creatively, using new and unconventional ideas rather than traditional approaches
vocabulary.definition_vi: suy nghĩ sáng tạo, phá cách, không rập khuôn
vocabulary.example: Modern employers value candidates who can think outside the box to solve complex problems.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung một chiếc hộp (box) tượng trưng cho lối suy nghĩ thông thường — 'thinking outside the box' là bước ra khỏi khuôn khổ đó.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cụm từ ẩn dụ chỉ rào cản vô hình ngăn cản một số nhóm người thăng tiến lên vị trí lãnh đạo cao cấp.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Many women still struggle to break through the **glass ceiling** to reach executive board levels.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Một trần nhà bằng kính trong suốt nên nhìn thấy cơ hội phía trên nhưng không thể chạm tới, ẩn dụ cho rào cản vô hình.
vocabulary.common_error: Thường dùng *the glass ceiling* và động từ *break through/shatter*; không dùng cho mọi trở ngại hữu hình hoặc quy định chính thức.
vocabulary.definition_en: an unofficial, invisible barrier that prevents certain groups, especially women, from rising to senior positions
vocabulary.definition_vi: rào cản vô hình (trần kính) ngăn cản một số nhóm người, đặc biệt là phụ nữ, thăng tiến lên vị trí cao
vocabulary.example: Many women still struggle to break through the glass ceiling to reach executive board levels.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Một trần nhà bằng kính (glass ceiling) trong suốt nên nhìn thấy cơ hội phía trên nhưng không thể chạm tới — ẩn dụ cho rào cản vô hình.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khoản tiền lớn được trao cho nhân viên, thường là cấp quản lý, khi họ rời công ty hoặc nghỉ hưu.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Upon his early retirement, the director received a massive **golden handshake** as compensation for his years of service.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Một cái bắt tay vàng khi chia tay công ty tượng trưng cho món quà chia tay hậu hĩnh bằng tiền.
vocabulary.common_error: *Golden handshake* là khoản chi trả khi rời công ty, khác *golden hello* (thưởng khi gia nhập) và *golden parachute* (bảo vệ lãnh đạo khi thâu tóm).
vocabulary.definition_en: a generous sum of money given to an employee, typically a senior executive, upon leaving a company, often at retirement
vocabulary.definition_vi: khoản tiền thưởng lớn khi nghỉ hưu hoặc rời công ty (thường dành cho cấp cao)
vocabulary.example: Upon his early retirement, the director received a massive golden handshake as compensation for his years of service.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Một 'cái bắt tay vàng' (golden handshake) khi chia tay công ty — món quà chia tay hậu hĩnh bằng tiền.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hiện tượng thị trường lao động bị chia thành hai cực kỹ năng cao và thấp, trong khi việc làm kỹ năng trung bình dần biến mất.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Labour-market polarisation** has been illustrated through the hollowing-out of routine, mid-skill occupations such as clerical work.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Polar' gợi hai cực đối lập Bắc–Nam — thị trường lao động cũng bị chia thành hai cực, mất đi phần giữa.
vocabulary.common_error: Chú ý chính tả Anh-Anh: 'polarisation' (Anh) khác với 'polarization' (Mỹ) — dùng '-isation' theo chuẩn British spelling.
vocabulary.definition_en: the hollowing-out of mid-skill jobs in an economy, with employment growth concentrated instead at the high-skill and low-skill ends
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự phân cực thị trường lao động (mất dần việc làm kỹ năng trung bình, tập trung vào hai cực cao và thấp)
vocabulary.example: Labour-market polarisation has been illustrated through the hollowing-out of routine, mid-skill occupations such as clerical work.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Polar' gợi hai cực đối lập (Bắc–Nam) — thị trường lao động cũng bị chia thành hai cực: kỹ năng cao và kỹ năng thấp, mất đi phần giữa.
